newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Foreign investment in Israel rose last year.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Israel rose last year.

text.p: Foreign investment into Israel rose to $2.594 billion in 1996 from $2.205 billion in 1995, with most of the money pouring into Israeli share listing in New York, the central Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.

Overall, capital inflows fell sharply to $4.360 billion from $7.895 billion, but the Bank of Israel said the decline was mainly due to reduced capital inflows by Israelis taking foreign currency or foreign currency-linked loans.

Capital inflows by Israelis dropped to $1.769 billion last year from $5.690 billion in 1995. Foreign exchange-linked credits by Israelis meanwhile fell to $2.141 billion from $5.830 billion although direct forex credit from overseas grew to $1.48 billion from $470 million.
The Bank of Israel attributed the decline in forex borrowing to increased expectations for a devaluation of the shekel last year.
In early March, the central bank admitted that expectations for a devaluation had risen again, spurring a renewed wave of forex borrowing.

Foreign financial investment into Israel grew to $1.428 billion last year from $992 million in 1995, the central bank said. Foreigners invested $761 million into Israeli initial public offerings, almost entirely in shares listed in New York, up from $325 million in 1995.

Foreign investment in traded shares listed overseas rose to $326 million from $279 million in 1995 while investment in Tel Aviv Stock Exchange-listed shares dropped to $341 million from $386 million, the central bank said.
Foreign direct investment grew slightly to $1.249 billion from $1.219 billion in 1995.
Outward financial investment by Israelis fell to $29 million from $108 million in 1995, while outward direct investment grew to $671 million from $606 million.

The Bank of Israel said Israel's net foreign debt contracted by approximately $500 million to $19.9 billion at the end of 1996. It added that net foreign debt now equalled 22 percent of gross domestic product, down from 23 percent a year earlier.
